lessons.title: Introduction to Python
lessons.summary: Welcome to the Python course!

blocks.content: Welcome to the Python course!
You're about to start learning Python—one of the most popular and widely used programming languages in the world.
It's not just easy to learn—it's also incredibly powerful.
People use it to build websites, create apps, analyze data, automate tasks, and even work on AI.
Whether you're aiming for a career in tech or just curious about coding, Python is a great place to start.
On this page, you don't need to write any code yet.
See the editor on the right?
You'll be using it soon to write your own Python code.
And don't worry—you can't break anything. Just follow along, explore, and have fun with it.
This course will guide you step by step in a friendly and easy way—no pressure, and no prior experience needed.

blocks.text: When you're ready, click Next Lesson, and we'll run your very first Python code together.

lessons.title: Strings are Fixed Values
lessons.summary: Remember the very first Python code you wrote?

blocks.content: Remember the very first Python code you wrote?
We asked you to type it exactly like that — and here's why.
In Python, strings are case sensitive. That means uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as completely different.
For example:

- "welcome" is not the same as "WELCOME"
- "welcome" is not the same as "Welcome"
- "welcome" is not the same as "WelCome"
The letters have to match exactly — same spelling, same case.
Similarly, spaces matter too.
Even a small space can change the string completely.

- "welcome" is not the same as "wel come" (there's a space in the middle)
- "welcome" is not the same as " welcome" (space at the beginning)
- "welcome" is not the same as "welcome " (space at the end)
To us, it might look similar — but Python sees it as something totally different.
So always double-check your spelling, your casing, and your spacing.
Next, let's learn about numbers in Python.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.summary: The two common types of numbers in Python are:

blocks.content: The two common types of numbers in Python are:
Integers are numbers without decimal points. They can be positive, negative, or zero. Examples include 5, -11, 0 and 12.
Floating-point numbers contain decimal points. Like integers, they can also be positive, negative, or zero. Examples include 2.5, 6.76, 0.0, and -9.45.
You'll learn how to print these numbers—but first, take a quick quiz on floating-point numbers.

lessons.title: Introduction to Comments
lessons.summary: As you start writing more code, you might want to add short explanations inside your program—not for the computer, but for yourself or anyone else reading it later.

blocks.content: As you start writing more code, you might want to add short explanations inside your program—not for the computer, but for yourself or anyone else reading it later.
Suppose you write this line in your code:
This will simply print the number 34.0.
Now let's say you want to explain what this number means. Maybe it's the temperature or the result of a calculation. You might try writing it like this:
But Python won't understand that extra text, and it will give you an error.
So how do you include extra information in your code without breaking it?
That's where comments come in. Comments let you add helpful notes right inside your code, and Python will simply ignore them when running the program.
You don't need to worry about how to write them just yet.

blocks.text: Click Next Lesson to learn how to add comments properly in Python.

lessons.title: Python Comments
lessons.summary: In Python, we use the # symbol to write comments in our code.

blocks.content: In Python, we use the # symbol to write comments in our code.
On the last page, we saw that writing something like this:
will give you an error. That's because Python tries to read everything on the line, and it doesn't know what to do with the extra text.
But sometimes, you do want to write a quick note to explain what a line of code is doing. To do that without causing an error, you can use a comment.
Just add a # before the explanation, like this:

Now Python will run the first part (print(34.0)) and completely ignore anything after the #. In fact, Python skips any line that starts with #—it doesn't run it, and it won't appear in the output at all.
Next, you'll look at more examples of comments.

lessons.title: Legal Variables Name
lessons.summary: There are certain rules for naming variables. Let's learn about them.

blocks.content: There are certain rules for naming variables. Let's learn about them.
A variable name can only consist of three elements:

- alphabets
- numbers
- underscores
Do not use spaces or any other symbols when naming a variable. If a variable name consists of two words, separate them with an underscore, _ or use camelCase.
For example, first name and first-name are not valid variable names, but first_name and firstName are valid.

blocks.alt: If the name consists of two or more words, use underscores to separate them. We cannot use spaces or other symbols in variable names.
blocks.caption: Figure: Legal and Illegal Variable Names

blocks.content: It's important to note that a valid variable name doesn't necessarily mean it's a good name. For example, lkc is a valid variable name, but it's not meaningful.
Refer to this article to learn how and why you should assign clear and meaningful names to variables.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes (I)
lessons.summary: Before moving to the next lesson, let's discuss common mistakes beginners may make.

blocks.content: Before moving to the next lesson, let's discuss common mistakes beginners may make.
1. Spelling Error
This one is obvious—using wrong variable names and misspelling words will cause an error. For example:

blocks.code:
annual_income = 95000
# error because of a spelling mistake
print(annual_icome)
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code: NameError: name 'annual_icome' is not defined. Did you mean: 'annual_income'?
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: In most cases, carefully reading the error message helps us fix these problems easily.
For instance, the output clearly states that annual_icome is not defined in line 4.
Also, Python is case-sensitive. So annual_income and Annual_income are also not the same.
The same rule applies to print() as well—writing it as Print() or any other way will result in an error.
2. Adding Spaces at the Beginning
In Python, indentation has a specific meaning. So, if we add unnecessary spaces at the beginning, we will get an error. For example,
If you run the program, you will get an error because there are spaces before print().

lessons.title: Common Mistakes (II)
lessons.summary: We have seen many beginners make this mistake. They usually forget to close the string with quotation marks. For example,

blocks.content: We have seen many beginners make this mistake. They usually forget to close the string with quotation marks. For example,
Here, Python doesn't understand what "Hello is.
"Hello is not a string because it doesn't have the closing quotation mark. And it's not a variable because we cannot use quotation marks in variable names.

blocks.text: 4. Forgetting Commas in the print() Function

blocks.content: Here, Python interprets "Age:" age as a single item. Since it's neither a string nor a variable, we get an error.

blocks.text: 5. Forgetting to use f in a f-string

blocks.content: If you forget to include f before the quotation marks, the string is treated as a normal string. As a result, {age} is interpreted as plain text instead of being evaluated as a variable.
Avoid these five common mistakes and enjoy a smoother programming experience.
You can improve your Python skills by practicing regularly and staying mindful of common mistakes. To learn more about printing in Python, check out the Printing Basics in Python article.
